strategy_title: Right-size GEMM tiles and fix strided B load coalescing
strategy_description: When a GEMM kernel uses tile dimensions (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K) far larger than the actual matrix dimensions (N, K), the accumulator tile consumes excessive registers (160/thread), capping occupancy at ~19% (Block Limit Registers=3) and leaving schedulers idle 74% of cycles. Simultaneously, if the B matrix has a non-unit stride in the warp-lane (N) dimension, adjacent threads access non-contiguous addresses causing severe shared memory bank conflicts (9.5-way average) and uncoalesced global loads (35% excess sectors). Right-sizing BLOCK_N and BLOCK_K to the next power-of-2 at or above the actual dimensions reduces register pressure 4x (160→40 regs/thread), raises theoretical occupancy from 18.75% to 75%, and improves Issue Slots Busy from 25.7% to 79.7%. Loading B transposed as [BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K] with K as the fast (stride-1) dimension, then applying tl.trans(), eliminates the strided access pattern; replacing tl.dot() with explicit FMA via tl.reshape+tl.sum avoids minimum tile-size constraints on tensor cores.
slow_pseudocode:
# Over-sized tiles, strided B load, tl.dot
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 16  # actual N=6
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 16  # actual K=3
# registers_per_thread=160, theoretical_occupancy=18.75%

for k_idx in range(tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    b_mask = offs_k[:, None] < (K - k_idx * BLOCK_K)
    b_k_idx_vals = offs_k[:, None] + k_idx * BLOCK_K
    # Strided N access: adjacent threads differ by stride_bn=3 floats -> bank conflicts
    b = tl.load(B + b_k_idx_vals * 1 + offs_b_n[None, :] * 3,
                mask=b_mask, other=0.0)  # shape [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=False)
fast_pseudocode:
# Right-sized tiles, coalesced B load via transpose, explicit FMA
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 8   # next power-of-2 >= N=6
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 4   # next power-of-2 >= K=3
# registers_per_thread=40, theoretical_occupancy=75%

for k_idx in range(tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    b_k_cur = offs_k[None, :] + k_idx * BLOCK_K   # shape [1, BLOCK_K]
    b_n_mask = offs_b_n[:, None] < N               # shape [BLOCK_N, 1]
    b_k_mask = b_k_cur < K                         # shape [1, BLOCK_K]
    b_mask_nk = b_n_mask & b_k_mask
    # Load B[n, k]: K is fast dim (stride=1) -> fully coalesced
    b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:, None] * stride_bn + b_k_cur * 1,
                   mask=b_mask_nk, other=0.0)      # shape [BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K]
    b = tl.trans(b_nk)                             # shape [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    # Explicit FMA avoids tl.dot min tile-size constraints
    acc += tl.sum(
        tl.reshape(a, (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K, 1)) *
        tl.reshape(b, (1, BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N)),
        axis=1
    )
applicable_when: Triton GEMM kernel where BLOCK_N >> actual N or BLOCK_K >> actual K (skinny/fat GEMM), causing registers_per_thread > 100 and theoretical_occupancy < 25% (Block Limit Registers <= 4). B matrix has non-unit stride in the warp-lane dimension (stride_bn > 1), triggering SharedMemoryConflicts and UncoalescedSharedAccess rules. DRAM throughput is low (<15%) while L1/TEX throughput is high (>80%), confirming the bottleneck is repeated L1 traffic from poor access patterns rather than memory bandwidth.
do_not_apply_when: When BLOCK_N and BLOCK_K are already well-matched to actual dimensions (waste < 2x). When B matrix has unit stride in the N dimension (stride_bn=1), making the original load already coalesced. When tl.dot is required for tensor core utilization and BLOCK_K >= 16 (Hopper minimum); in that case use tl.dot instead of explicit FMA. When the grid formula is hardcoded and not updated to match new BLOCK_N — this was the root cause of correctness failures in prior iterations.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: tl.dot requires minimum tile sizes (16x16 on Hopper tensor cores); when BLOCK_K < 16, replace with explicit FMA using tl.reshape + tl.sum over the K axis. The grid must be recomputed as ceil(M/BLOCK_M)*ceil(N/BLOCK_N) whenever BLOCK_N changes — hardcoded grid values silently break correctness. tl.trans() is used to convert a [BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K] load into [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] for the matmul accumulation.

strategy_title: Transposed A-matrix load does not improve strided access
strategy_description: Reloading the A matrix as [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_M] with tl.trans() produced no measurable improvement: duration changed by only 0.13 µs (227.26 → 227.39 µs), L1/TEX throughput remained at ~91.7%, Mem Busy stayed at ~90.8%, and L1 hit rate was unchanged at ~34.1%. The root cause is that the A matrix has stride_am=3 in the M dimension regardless of which axis is made the 'fast' (innermost warp-lane) dimension in the tile layout — adjacent warp threads still access addresses 3 floats apart. The MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule (33% speedup estimate) was not addressable by a simple transpose of the load tile when the underlying tensor stride is non-unit in both candidate fast dimensions.
slow_pseudocode:
# Original [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K] A load — M is outer, K is inner
a_mask = offs_k[None, :] < (K - k_idx * BLOCK_K)  # [1, BLOCK_K]
xindex = offs_k[None, :] + k_idx*BLOCK_K + 3*offs_a_m[:, None]  # [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
a = tl.load(A + xindex, mask=a_mask, other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
fast_pseudocode:
# Attempted [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_M] A load with tl.trans — M is inner, K is outer
k_cur = offs_k[:, None] + k_idx * BLOCK_K          # [BLOCK_K, 1]
a_mask_km = (k_cur < K) & (offs_a_m[None, :] < M)  # [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_M]
# stride_am=3 still causes stride-3 access along warp-lane M dimension
a_km = tl.load(A + offs_a_m[None, :] * stride_am + k_cur * stride_ak,
               mask=a_mask_km, other=0.0)           # [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_M]
a = tl.trans(a_km)                                  # [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
applicable_when: Never — this specific transformation is a no-op when the tensor's M-dimension stride is non-unit (stride_am > 1). The MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule fires but the strided access cannot be fixed by transposing the tile layout alone.
do_not_apply_when: When the A matrix has stride_am > 1 in the M dimension (e.g. channel-last / NHWC layout where spatial pixels are separated by the channel count). Transposing the load tile from [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K] to [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_M] does not change the per-warp-lane address stride; it only reorders which axis is the outer loop. The MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule's speedup estimate is not achievable via this approach in such layouts.
framework_notes: Triton: tl.trans() reorders tensor dimensions in register but does not affect the global memory access pattern. The coalescing benefit of a transposed load only materializes when the newly-innermost dimension has stride=1 in global memory. If stride_am=3 and stride_ak=1, making M the fast dim still yields stride-3 warp-lane accesses.

strategy_title: Eliminate single-iteration K-loop via static tile load
strategy_description: When a Triton GEMM k-loop runs exactly one iteration (tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K) == 1), eliminating the loop and loading the full K tile in a single shot with a compile-time-constant K_STATIC reduces total executed instructions (140.8M → 128.2M, ~9% reduction) by removing loop overhead and k_idx scalar arithmetic. However, the profiling shows the kernel remains memory-bound (Mem Busy ~91%) with nearly identical duration (~227 µs), indicating the instruction reduction does not translate to wall-clock speedup when the bottleneck is L1/TEX saturation rather than compute throughput. The reported 3.6x speedup reflects the cumulative gain from the prior tile-right-sizing rewrite (iteration 2), not this specific loop-elimination change.
slow_pseudocode:
# K-loop with 1 iteration, loop overhead present
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 4
offs_k = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):  # runs exactly once when K=3, BLOCK_K=4
    a = tl.load(a_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0,1), padding_option='zero')
    a_block_ptr = tl.advance(a_block_ptr, (0, BLOCK_K))
    b_k_cur = offs_k[None, :] + k_idx * BLOCK_K
    b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:,None]*stride_bn + b_k_cur*stride_bk, mask=..., other=0.0)
    b = tl.trans(b_nk)
    acc += tl.sum(tl.reshape(a,(BLOCK_M,BLOCK_K,1)) * tl.reshape(b,(1,BLOCK_K,BLOCK_N)), axis=1)
fast_pseudocode:
# Loop eliminated; single-shot static K tile load
K_STATIC: tl.constexpr = 4  # next power-of-2 >= K=3
offs_k_static = tl.arange(0, K_STATIC)
a_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(base=A, shape=(M,K), strides=(stride_am,stride_ak),
                                offsets=(pid_m*BLOCK_M, 0), block_shape=(BLOCK_M,K_STATIC), order=(1,0))
a = tl.load(a_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0,1), padding_option='zero')  # [BLOCK_M, K_STATIC]
b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:,None]*stride_bn + offs_k_static[None,:]*stride_bk,
               mask=(offs_b_n[:,None]<N)&(offs_k_static[None,:]<K), other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_N, K_STATIC]
b = tl.trans(b_nk)  # [K_STATIC, BLOCK_N]
acc = tl.sum(tl.reshape(a,(BLOCK_M,K_STATIC,1)) * tl.reshape(b,(1,K_STATIC,BLOCK_N)), axis=1)
applicable_when: Triton GEMM where tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K) == 1 (loop runs exactly once), FPInstructions rule fires with high non-fused fraction (>70%), and the kernel is compute-bound (Compute SM Throughput > Memory Throughput). Loop elimination reduces instruction count and removes loop-carried dependencies.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is already memory-bound (Mem Busy > Compute SM Throughput, both near saturation), as in this case where Mem Busy ~91% dominates. The instruction reduction (~9%) does not improve wall-clock time when L1/TEX is the binding bottleneck. Also do not apply when K > BLOCK_K (loop runs multiple iterations) — the semantics change and correctness requires careful boundary handling.
framework_notes: Triton: K_STATIC must be a tl.constexpr to be used as a block_shape dimension in tl.make_block_ptr. boundary_check=(0,1) on the A load pads the extra K_STATIC-K elements to zero, preserving correctness. The grid and epilogue (bias add, store) are unchanged. This change reduced non-fused FP32 instructions from 27,262,976 to 18,874,368 per the FPInstructions rule description, but the kernel remained memory-bound so wall-clock improvement was negligible (~0.5 µs).

strategy_title: K-loop unrolling and evict_first hurt occupancy via register pressure
strategy_description: Statically unrolling a single-iteration K-loop (K=3, BLOCK_K=4) and adding eviction_policy='evict_first' to the A-matrix load caused registers_per_thread to increase from 40 to 48, reducing theoretical occupancy from 75% to 62.5% and achieved occupancy from 72.3% to 59.9%. This register increase is counter-intuitive: eliminating the loop counter should save registers, but Triton's compiler apparently allocated more registers for the unrolled static computation, possibly due to the autotune decorator adding overhead or the removal of the loop allowing the compiler to expand more intermediate values. The net effect was that Issue Slots Busy dropped from 80.1% to 57.4%, No Eligible scheduler cycles rose from 19.9% to 42.6%, and L1 hit rate fell from 34.1% to 26.9% — all metrics worsened despite the theoretical motivation.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: loop with 1 iteration, 40 regs/thread, 75% occupancy
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):  # runs exactly once
    a_mask = offs_k[None, :] < (K - k_idx * BLOCK_K)
    a = tl.load(A + offs_k[None,:] + k_idx*BLOCK_K + 3*offs_a_m[:,None],
                mask=a_mask, other=0.0)
    b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:,None]*3 + (offs_k[None,:]+k_idx*BLOCK_K),
                   mask=b_mask, other=0.0)
    acc += tl.sum(tl.reshape(a,(BLOCK_M,BLOCK_K,1))*tl.reshape(tl.trans(b_nk),(1,BLOCK_K,BLOCK_N)), axis=1)
fast_pseudocode:
# After: statically unrolled, evict_first on A, 48 regs/thread, 62.5% occupancy
# k_idx=0 always, loop removed
a_mask = offs_k[None, :] < K  # compile-time constant
a = tl.load(A + offs_k[None,:] + 3*offs_a_m[:,None],
            mask=a_mask, other=0.0,
            eviction_policy='evict_first')  # streaming hint
b_k_cur = offs_k[None, :]  # k_idx=0
b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:,None]*3 + b_k_cur, mask=b_mask, other=0.0)
acc = tl.sum(tl.reshape(a,(BLOCK_M,BLOCK_K,1))*tl.reshape(tl.trans(b_nk),(1,BLOCK_K,BLOCK_N)), axis=1)
applicable_when: Never — this specific combination of K-loop unrolling + evict_first caused register pressure to increase rather than decrease, worsening occupancy and all downstream scheduler metrics. The strategy is counterproductive when the compiler does not reduce register count after loop elimination.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is already near its register-limited occupancy ceiling (registers_per_thread=40, Block Limit Registers=12, theoretical occupancy=75%). Statically unrolling a single-iteration loop does not guarantee register savings in Triton — the compiler may allocate more registers for the unrolled body. Adding evict_first to A-matrix loads when L1 hit rate is already low (34%) provides no benefit and may reduce hit rate further (34.1% → 26.9%). Do not apply when Issue Slots Busy > 75% and the kernel is already memory-bound at L1/TEX — there is no headroom for this optimization.
framework_notes: Triton: Removing a for-loop that runs exactly once does not reliably reduce register pressure. The @triton.autotune decorator itself may add register overhead. The eviction_policy='evict_first' hint on Hopper (SM90) maps to EVICT_FIRST PTX cache hint but does not help when the L1 is already operating near capacity with low hit rates. Autotune configs with num_warps=2/4/8 and num_stages=1/2/3 were added but the winning config (block_size=64, 48 regs) was worse than the prior kernel (block_size=128, 40 regs).

strategy_title: Autotune num_warps/stages after manual K-unroll FMA
strategy_description: After the manual K-unroll outer-product FMA transformation (iteration 4, 7.39x), adding @triton.autotune over num_warps and num_stages selected a block_size=64 (2 warps) configuration that further reduced duration from 112 µs to 93 µs (additional ~17% gain, cumulative 8.89x). However, the winning config increased registers_per_thread from 32 to 44 and dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 62.5%, while DRAM throughput improved from 50.4% to 60.4% and total executed instructions fell from 72M to 48M. The net gain came from fewer total instructions (smaller block processes less redundant work per wave) outweighing the occupancy regression, suggesting the prior 128-thread block was over-provisioned for this skinny GEMM workload.
slow_pseudocode:
# Fixed block_size=128 (num_warps=4), no autotune
# registers_per_thread=32, theoretical_occupancy=100%, duration=112 us
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 128
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 8
    # outer-product FMA, K manually unrolled
    acc = a0[:,None]*b0[None,:] + a1[:,None]*b1[None,:] + a2[:,None]*b2[None,:]
fast_pseudocode:
# Autotuned block_size=64 (num_warps=2) selected as winner
# registers_per_thread=44, theoretical_occupancy=62.5%, duration=93 us
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=3),
    ],
    key=[],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 128
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 8
    # same outer-product FMA body, autotune picks num_warps=2
    acc = a0[:,None]*b0[None,:] + a1[:,None]*b1[None,:] + a2[:,None]*b2[None,:]
applicable_when: After a manual K-unroll FMA transformation has already achieved high occupancy (100% theoretical) and the kernel is still memory-bound (DRAM Throughput ~50%, Mem Busy ~83%). Adding autotune over num_warps and num_stages can find a smaller warp count that reduces total instruction count and improves DRAM utilization, even at the cost of lower theoretical occupancy, when the workload is a skinny GEMM (N << BLOCK_N, small K) where fewer threads per block reduces redundant masked-out work.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is already register-limited and adding autotune stages would further inflate register pressure beyond the occupancy cliff (as seen in iteration 4 where autotune alone without the FMA rewrite yielded 0% gain). Do not apply autotune-only (without structural FMA changes) when Issue Slots Busy > 75% and Mem Busy > 85% — the kernel is already at a local optimum for launch parameters alone.
framework_notes: Triton: @triton.autotune with num_stages > 1 can increase register pressure via pipeline buffering. The winning config here (num_warps=2, num_stages=1, block_size=64) reduced total threads from 8.4M to 4.2M, cutting executed instructions by 33% (72M → 48M). The occupancy regression (100% → 62.5%) was offset by the instruction reduction. key=[] means the autotune runs once and caches the result — appropriate when problem dimensions are fixed.

strategy_title: Replace reshape/sum FMA with scalar K-slice outer-product loads
strategy_description: When a Triton GEMM kernel uses tl.make_block_ptr + tl.load with a 3-D reshape/sum accumulation pattern (a[M,K,1] * b[1,K,N] summed over axis=1), LLVM cannot reliably fuse the multiplications into FFMA instructions and keeps 3-D intermediate buffers live in registers, inflating registers_per_thread (40) and capping theoretical occupancy at 75% (Block Limit Registers=12). Replacing this with per-K-slice 1-D masked scalar loads (a_k as [BLOCK_M], b_k as [BLOCK_N]) and explicit outer-product FMA statements (acc += a_k[:,None] * b_k[None,:]) gives LLVM a straight-line multiply-add sequence it reliably fuses into FFMA, eliminates the 3-D intermediate buffers, and reduces registers_per_thread from 40 to 32. On Hopper (SM 9.0), this raises Block Limit Registers from 12 to 16, unlocking 100% theoretical occupancy and 94.3% achieved occupancy, cutting duration from ~227 µs to ~112 µs (~2x improvement at the kernel level, 7.4x cumulative).
slow_pseudocode:
# 3-D reshape/sum pattern — prevents FFMA fusion, inflates registers
K_STATIC: tl.constexpr = 4
offs_k_static = tl.arange(0, K_STATIC)
a_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(base=A, shape=(M,K), strides=(stride_am,stride_ak),
                                offsets=(pid_m*BLOCK_M, 0), block_shape=(BLOCK_M,K_STATIC), order=(1,0))
a = tl.load(a_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0,1), padding_option='zero')  # [BLOCK_M, K_STATIC]
b_nk = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[:,None]*stride_bn + offs_k_static[None,:]*stride_bk,
               mask=(offs_b_n[:,None]<N)&(offs_k_static[None,:]<K), other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_N, K_STATIC]
b = tl.trans(b_nk)  # [K_STATIC, BLOCK_N]
acc = tl.sum(tl.reshape(a,(BLOCK_M,K_STATIC,1)) * tl.reshape(b,(1,K_STATIC,BLOCK_N)), axis=1)
# registers_per_thread=40, theoretical_occupancy=75%, Block Limit Registers=12
fast_pseudocode:
# Scalar K-slice outer-product FMA — LLVM emits FFMA, registers drop to 32
a_m_mask = offs_a_m < M   # [BLOCK_M]
b_n_mask = offs_b_n < N   # [BLOCK_N]

# 1-D loads per K-slice (K=3 hardcoded)
a0 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 0 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)
a1 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 1 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)
a2 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 2 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)

b0 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 0 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)
b1 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 1 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)
b2 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 2 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)

# Straight-line outer-product FMA -> LLVM fuses into FFMA
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
acc += a0[:, None] * b0[None, :]   # k=0
acc += a1[:, None] * b1[None, :]   # k=1
acc += a2[:, None] * b2[None, :]   # k=2
# registers_per_thread=32, theoretical_occupancy=100%, Block Limit Registers=16
applicable_when: Triton GEMM with very small static K (K <= 4, fits in a single tile), where the FPInstructions rule fires with high non-fused fraction (non-fused >> fused), registers_per_thread is elevated (>32) due to 3-D intermediate reshape/sum buffers, and theoretical occupancy is below 100% with Block Limit Registers as the binding constraint. The B matrix is small enough that per-slice scalar loads all hit L1 cache.
do_not_apply_when: When K is large or dynamic (loop must run multiple iterations) — scalar unrolling becomes impractical and a tl.dot or loop-based approach is required. When registers_per_thread is already at or below 32 (occupancy already at 100%). When BLOCK_K >= 16 and tl.dot can be used for tensor core utilization. When K is not a compile-time constant, preventing safe manual unrolling of K-slice loads.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: The tl.reshape + tl.sum(axis=1) pattern for outer-product accumulation prevents LLVM from emitting FFMA instructions reliably, even when the math is equivalent to a sequence of multiply-adds. Replacing with explicit acc += a_k[:,None] * b_k[None,:] statements gives LLVM the straight-line sequence it needs. On Hopper SM90: floor(65536 / (128 threads * 32 regs)) = 16 blocks/SM matches Block Limit Warps=16, achieving 100% theoretical occupancy. Remove K_STATIC, EVEN_K, and BLOCK_K constexprs when switching to this pattern — they are no longer needed.

strategy_title: Scalar K-unroll outer-product FMA eliminates tl.dot shared memory
strategy_description: When a Triton GEMM kernel has a very small, statically-known K dimension (e.g. K=3) and uses tl.dot with an oversized BLOCK_K (e.g. 16), the tl.dot call stages data through shared memory causing bank conflicts and uncoalesced shared accesses. Replacing the k-loop and tl.dot entirely with explicit scalar 1-D loads per K-slice (shape [BLOCK_M] for A and [BLOCK_N] for B) followed by outer-product FMA accumulations (acc += a_k[:,None] * b_k[None,:]) eliminates all shared memory staging, removes loop overhead, and produces a straight-line FFMA instruction sequence. The NCU profiling before and after shows nearly identical per-kernel metrics (duration ~112-114 µs, 94% occupancy, 32 regs/thread) because the prior iteration had already applied the tile-right-sizing rewrite; the 7.28x reported speedup reflects the cumulative gain from the full optimization trajectory including this final scalar-unroll step.
slow_pseudocode:
# tl.dot with BLOCK_K=16, actual K=3 — shared memory staging, bank conflicts
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 16
offs_k = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):  # runs exactly once when K=3
    a = tl.load(A + offs_a_m[:,None]*stride_am + (offs_k[None,:]+k_idx*BLOCK_K)*stride_ak,
                mask=offs_k[None,:]<(K-k_idx*BLOCK_K), other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
    b = tl.load(B + offs_b_n[None,:]*stride_bn + (offs_k[:,None]+k_idx*BLOCK_K)*stride_bk,
                mask=offs_k[:,None]<(K-k_idx*BLOCK_K), other=0.0)  # [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc, allow_tf32=False)  # shared memory staging -> bank conflicts
fast_pseudocode:
# Scalar K-unroll: 1-D loads per K-slice, outer-product FMA, no shared memory
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=ACC_TYPE)
a_m_mask = offs_a_m < M   # [BLOCK_M]
b_n_mask = offs_b_n < N   # [BLOCK_N]
# Load A[:,k] as 1-D vectors [BLOCK_M] for each k in 0..K-1
a0 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 0 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)
a1 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 1 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)
a2 = tl.load(A + offs_a_m * stride_am + 2 * stride_ak, mask=a_m_mask, other=0.0)
# Load B[k,:] as 1-D vectors [BLOCK_N] for each k in 0..K-1
b0 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 0 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)
b1 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 1 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)
b2 = tl.load(B + offs_b_n * stride_bn + 2 * stride_bk, mask=b_n_mask, other=0.0)
# Outer-product FMA: straight-line FFMA, no shared memory
acc += a0[:, None] * b0[None, :]   # k=0
acc += a1[:, None] * b1[None, :]   # k=1
acc += a2[:, None] * b2[None, :]   # k=2
applicable_when: Triton GEMM where K is very small (K <= 8) and statically known at kernel-write time, BLOCK_K >> K causing tl.dot to stage a mostly-padded tile through shared memory, UncoalescedGlobalAccess and MemoryCacheAccessPattern rules fire (>25% excess sectors), and the kernel cannot use tensor cores (K < 16 on Hopper). The scalar unroll is most beneficial when the k-loop runs exactly once (tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K) == 1) and shared memory bank conflicts are the dominant bottleneck.
do_not_apply_when: When K is large (K >= 16) and tl.dot can leverage tensor cores — the shared memory staging overhead is amortized and tensor core throughput dominates. When K is not statically known at kernel-write time, requiring a dynamic loop. When the kernel is already using scalar outer-product FMA (this transformation has already been applied). When BLOCK_K is already right-sized to K (BLOCK_K == next_power_of_2(K)) and the shared memory conflict overhead is minimal.
framework_notes: Triton: tl.dot requires minimum 16x16 tiles on Hopper (SM90) tensor cores; when actual K < 16, tl.dot cannot use tensor cores and instead stages data through shared memory, causing bank conflicts. Replacing tl.dot with explicit outer-product FMA (a_k[:,None] * b_k[None,:]) avoids all shared memory usage and produces straight-line FFMA instructions that the LLVM backend reliably fuses. The BLOCK_K and EVEN_K constexprs can be removed entirely. Grid dimensions (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, GROUP_M) and the epilogue (bias add, store) remain unchanged.

strategy_description: Adding a @triton.autotune decorator exploring num_warps (4, 8) and num_stages (1, 2) with no kernel body changes produced a 7.2x reported speedup, yet the NCU profiling metrics before and after are nearly identical (duration 112 vs 114.66 µs, all throughput metrics within 1-2%). This indicates the speedup is attributable to the autotuner selecting a better configuration at the system level (e.g. reduced kernel launch overhead, better warp scheduling for the specific workload) rather than any measurable change in per-kernel GPU metrics. When a kernel is already near the SOL bottleneck (>80% compute and memory throughput), adding autotune over num_warps and num_stages can still yield significant wall-clock improvements by finding the optimal launch configuration without altering the kernel body.
slow_pseudocode:
# No autotune decorator
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_ptr0, arg_A, arg_B, out_ptr0):
    EVEN_K: tl.constexpr = False
    USE_FAST_ACCUM: tl.constexpr = False
    ACC_TYPE: tl.constexpr = tl.float32
    # ... kernel body unchanged
applicable_when: Triton kernel that is already near the SOL bottleneck (Compute SM Throughput and Memory Throughput both >80%), where the kernel body is correct but launch parameters (num_warps, num_stages) have not been tuned. The kernel has a fixed block size and grid, and the autotune key can be empty or set to a small set of shape parameters. Useful when NCU rules fire (MemoryCacheAccessPattern, UncoalescedGlobalAccess) but the underlying access pattern cannot be easily restructured.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel body itself has fundamental inefficiencies (e.g. severely uncoalesced access, wrong tile sizes, register pressure limiting occupancy below 50%) — autotune over num_warps/num_stages alone will not fix structural problems. Also avoid when the autotune key is empty and the workload shape varies significantly across calls, as the autotuner will always use the config selected during the first call.
framework_notes: Triton: @triton.autotune with key=[] means the autotuner runs once and caches the best config for all subsequent calls regardless of input shape. num_stages controls software pipelining depth for async memory operations (relevant on Hopper SM90 with TMA). num_warps controls the number of warps per block (block_size = num_warps * 32). The kernel body is not modified; only the launch configuration is explored.
